name: Zimbabwe
summary: Southern Rhodesia’s white-minority government declared independence in 1965; after a liberation war, majority-ruled Zimbabwe was born in 1980 under Robert Mugabe.

knownFor.label: Great Zimbabwe ruins
knownFor.note: The country is named after them.

terrain.value: Most of the country lies on the Zimbabwean Plateau, over 1,000 m high, between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers.

climate.value: Subtropical highland, with a warm rainy season (November–March) and a cool dry winter; droughts are common.

resources.value: Fertile farmland, gold, platinum, chrome, coal and tobacco.

population.value: About 15 million people in the early 2020s.

disease.value: HIV was widespread in the 1990s–2000s, and a major cholera outbreak in 2008–09 killed several thousand people.

migration.value: Millions of Zimbabweans moved abroad, mainly to South Africa, after the economic collapse of the 2000s.

economicBase.value: Farming (tobacco, maize), mining (gold, platinum) and small trade, with a large informal sector.

tradeRoutes.value: Exports travel by road and rail through South Africa and Mozambique, since the country has no coast.

wealth.value: A low-income country; many people live in poverty after decades of economic crisis.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic, dominated by one party (ZANU–PF) since independence.

keyRulers.value: Robert Mugabe (prime minister from 1980, president from 1987 until 2017). Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: A 2017 coup d’état led to Mugabe’s resignation, and a successor became president.

institutions.value: A parliament of two houses, a constitution rewritten in 2013, and courts that critics say lack independence.

stability.value: In the Gukurahundi campaign, the Fifth Brigade killed thousands of civilians in Matabeleland; it officially ended in 1987.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Zimbabwe Defence Forces, which have played a part in politics since the 1980s.

majorWars.value: Zimbabwe took part in the war in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (1998–2002), which cost the economy hundreds of millions of dollars.

territoryChange.value: Zimbabwe’s borders have been unchanged since independence in 1980.

alliancesRivals.value: Under sanctions from the United States and the European Union since the early 2000s.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Literacy is among the highest in Africa, thanks to schooling expanded after 1980.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Railways link Harare and Bulawayo with Mozambique and South Africa; Victoria Falls is a major tourist site.

religion.value: Most people are Christian, mixing with traditional beliefs such as ancestor worship.

artsArchitecture.value: Shona stone sculpture, mbira music, and the medieval stone ruins of Great Zimbabwe.

sharedIdentity.value: The liberation struggle (chimurenga) is central to national identity, though Shona and Ndebele differences remain.

dailyLife.value: Many families farm small plots or work in towns; sadza (maize porridge) with relish is the daily staple.

ideasReligions.value: The ideals of liberation, land reform and nationalism shaped politics after 1980.

colonisation.value: Ruled by the British South Africa Company from 1890, then the self-governing British colony of Southern Rhodesia (1923); its white minority government declared independence as Rhodesia in 1965.

outcome.value: Zimbabwe continues as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
